questions.q: How does this lesson describe SOAR's relationship to the analyst role?
options: A force multiplier -- it removes repetitive work so analysts handle more volume, not a replacement for the role
A complete replacement for human analysts in a mature SOC
An unrelated tool that has no effect on analyst workload
A tool used only during analyst training, never in production
questions.explain: SOAR offloads the repeatable, well-understood work, which increases what the same analyst team can handle.

questions.q: Why can't a playbook handle a genuinely novel attack pattern?
options: There's no pre-built decision branch, because nobody has worked out the correct response to something that's never happened before
Novel attacks never generate any alerts at all
Playbooks are specifically designed only for novel, unseen attacks
Novel attacks always match an existing playbook branch automatically
questions.explain: A playbook can only act on decision logic a human already defined in advance -- which doesn't exist for a truly novel situation.

questions.q: In the VP login example, what can't a SOAR tool know on its own?
options: Business context like the VP's travel itinerary or an ongoing deal that would explain the unusual login
The IP address the login came from
The exact timestamp of the login event
Whether the login event was logged by the SIEM at all
questions.explain: A tool sees the login event itself but has no way to know business context like travel plans -- that judgment call needs a human.

questions.q: Who is responsible for building, testing, and tuning a SOAR playbook's logic?
options: A human -- every playbook starts as a human decision about the correct response, tested and revised over time
The SOAR platform designs and updates its own playbooks with no human involvement
Playbooks never need any tuning once deployed
Only the original software vendor can ever modify a playbook
questions.explain: Playbook logic is human-designed and requires ongoing human tuning as new attack patterns and false-positive sources appear.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why might an organization keep a human sign-off step on certain high-stakes actions even when the technical decision could be automated?
options: The consequences (like cutting employee access or a legally sensitive disclosure) are serious enough to warrant deliberate human accountability
SOAR platforms are technically incapable of performing high-stakes actions
Human sign-off is required by every single playbook, regardless of stakes
High-stakes actions never occur in a real SOC
questions.explain: This is a deliberate accountability choice for serious-consequence actions, not a technical limitation of SOAR.
